Scope and reading plan

The current official Mathematics Unit 2 includes quadratic equations over real and complex numbers, root nature, coefficient–root relations, and forming equations from roots. This supplied chapter also uses rational inequalities, modulus, roots, and a variable-base power equation. The necessary domain rules are included.

Read in this order: degree and roots → completed square and graph → root relations → signs and restrictions → parameter questions.

Important for JEE Main labels a useful exam-level idea, not an invented formula-frequency statistic.

Convention for source Q20: at a negative base, we include ordinary integer powers wherever defined. This is why the candidate (−1)−48(-1)^{-48}(−1)−48 is valid. We explain the real-power domain rather than silently assuming every real exponent is allowed at a negative base.

Formula and concept bank

Concept C01 — What makes an equation quadratic?

Important for JEE Main. A quadratic equation has the form

ax2+bx+c=0,a≠0.\boxed{ax^2+bx+c=0,\qquad a\ne0}.ax2+bx+c=0,a=0​.

Its highest power of the unknown xxx is 222. The coefficients a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c are fixed while we solve for xxx. A letter such as kkk may act as a parameter: a coefficient whose allowed values the question asks us to find.

Let f(x)=ax2+bx+cf(x)=ax^2+bx+cf(x)=ax2+bx+c. A root rrr is an input making the output zero:

f(r)=0.f(r)=0.f(r)=0.

For example, f(x)=x2−4x+3f(x)=x^2-4x+3f(x)=x2−4x+3 has roots 1,31,31,3, because f(1)=f(3)=0f(1)=f(3)=0f(1)=f(3)=0.

The leading coefficient must be checked before dividing or using the quadratic formula. If a parameter makes a=0a=0a=0, the equation changes type:

Remaining equation What happens?
bx+c=0bx+c=0bx+c=0, b≠0b\ne0b=0 One root x=−c/bx=-c/bx=−c/b. It is linear, not quadratic.
0x+0=00x+0=00x+0=0 Every input solves it.
0x+c=00x+c=00x+c=0, c≠0c\ne0c=0 No input solves it.

In Q3, k=0k=0k=0 gives 4x=04x=04x=0. It has a real root, but it fails the separate requirement “is a quadratic equation.”

A useful distinction: an equation asks where f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0; an inequality asks where its output is positive or negative. Positive output does not mean positive input.

Concept C02 — Factor form and completed-square form show different things

Important for JEE Main. In factor form,

f(x)=a(x−α)(x−β).f(x)=a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta).f(x)=a(x−α)(x−β).

The product is zero if either factor is zero, so the roots are α,β\alpha,\betaα,β. The symbols are just names for the two roots.

For a general quadratic, complete the square:

f(x)=a(x+b2a)2−b2−4ac4a.\boxed{f(x)=a\left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2-\frac{b^2-4ac}{4a}}.f(x)=a(x+2ab​)2−4ab2−4ac​​.

Put

Δ=b2−4ac,h=−b2a,v=−Δ4a.\Delta=b^2-4ac,\qquad h=-\frac b{2a},\qquad v=-\frac{\Delta}{4a}.Δ=b2−4ac,h=−2ab​,v=−4aΔ​.

Then f(x)=a(x−h)2+vf(x)=a(x-h)^2+vf(x)=a(x−h)2+v. Its graph is a parabola, and (h,v)(h,v)(h,v) is the vertex, where it turns.

Read the graph: f(x)=(x−2)2−1f(x)=(x-2)^2-1f(x)=(x−2)2−1. At x=2x=2x=2, the square is zero and the output is smallest, −1-1−1. Equal steps left and right of 222 give equal squares, so the line x=2x=2x=2 is its symmetry axis.

  • If a>0a>0a>0, the graph opens upward.
  • If a<0a<0a<0, it opens downward.
  • The magnitude ∣a∣|a|∣a∣ changes the vertical scale.

Which form should I choose? Factor form makes roots and signs visible. Completed-square form makes the vertex, range, and minimum/maximum visible. Expanding is useful only when it reveals something we need.

Concept C03 — The discriminant tells us the nature of the roots

Important for JEE Main. Solving the completed-square equation gives

x=−b±Δ2a,Δ=b2−4ac.\boxed{x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2a}},\qquad\Delta=b^2-4ac.x=2a−b±Δ​​​,Δ=b2−4ac.

The symbol ±\pm± gives the two sign choices. For real coefficients:

Discriminant Roots Graph
Δ>0\Delta>0Δ>0 Two real and distinct roots. Crosses the horizontal axis twice.
Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0 Equal real roots; one distinct value. Touches the axis at its vertex.
Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0 A nonreal conjugate pair. Does not meet the real horizontal axis.

Read the words carefully.

real roots: Δ≥0,real and distinct: Δ>0.\boxed{\text{real roots: }\Delta\ge0},\qquad \boxed{\text{real and distinct: }\Delta>0}.real roots: Δ≥0​,real and distinct: Δ>0​.

For a repeated root, there are two roots counted with repetition but only one distinct solution. This is why a question saying “distinct” changes an endpoint.

For Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0 the roots are

−b±i−Δ2a.\frac{-b\pm i\sqrt{-\Delta}}{2a}.2a−b±i−Δ​​.

They are complex, not absent altogether; they are absent from the real xxx-axis.

Do not forget the leading coefficient: this classification assumes a≠0a\ne0a=0. A discriminant calculation cannot turn a linear equation into a quadratic.

Concept C04 — Always positive or negative: combine shape and crossings

Important for JEE Main. If a quadratic never meets the axis, its graph stays wholly above it or wholly below it. The sign of aaa decides which.

For a genuine real quadratic:

f(x)>0 for all real x  ⟺  a>0, Δ<0,\boxed{f(x)>0\text{ for all real }x \iff a>0,\ \Delta<0},f(x)>0 for all real x⟺a>0, Δ<0​, f(x)<0 for all real x  ⟺  a<0, Δ<0.\boxed{f(x)<0\text{ for all real }x \iff a<0,\ \Delta<0}.f(x)<0 for all real x⟺a<0, Δ<0​.

If equality is allowed,

f(x)≥0 ∀x  ⟺  a>0, Δ≤0,f(x)≤0 ∀x  ⟺  a<0, Δ≤0.\boxed{f(x)\ge0\ \forall x\iff a>0,\ \Delta\le0},\qquad \boxed{f(x)\le0\ \forall x\iff a<0,\ \Delta\le0}.f(x)≥0 ∀x⟺a>0, Δ≤0​,f(x)≤0 ∀x⟺a<0, Δ≤0​.

Why are both conditions needed? Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0 says “no axis crossing.” It does not say “above.” An upside-down graph can have no roots and still be negative everywhere.

The strict positive condition also follows from the vertex value −Δ/(4a)-\Delta/(4a)−Δ/(4a): with a>0a>0a>0, the minimum must be greater than zero. If Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0, the graph touches zero and strict positivity fails.

If a parameter makes the expression constant or linear, test that case separately. A positive constant is positive everywhere; a nonconstant real line cannot be positive for every real input.

Two useful input clues.

  • If a+b+c=0a+b+c=0a+b+c=0, then f(1)=0f(1)=0f(1)=0. The factors are (x−1)(ax−c)(x-1)(ax-c)(x−1)(ax−c) and the roots are 1,c/a1,c/a1,c/a.
  • If a−b+c=0a-b+c=0a−b+c=0, then f(−1)=0f(-1)=0f(−1)=0. The other root is −c/a-c/a−c/a.

These are substitutions, not magic formulas. For the first condition, b=−a−cb=-a-cb=−a−c, so Δ=(a−c)2≥0\Delta=(a-c)^2\ge0Δ=(a−c)2≥0 is another direct proof that the roots are real.

Concept C05 — Sum and product: find only the information asked

Important for JEE Main. Expand the factor form:

a(x−α)(x−β)=ax2−a(α+β)x+aαβ.a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta) =ax^2-a(\alpha+\beta)x+a\alpha\beta.a(x−α)(x−β)=ax2−a(α+β)x+aαβ.

Compare coefficients:

S=α+β=−ba,P=αβ=ca.\boxed{S=\alpha+\beta=-\frac ba,\qquad P=\alpha\beta=\frac ca}.S=α+β=−ab​,P=αβ=ac​​.

These are Viète's relations. They work for real or complex roots. They often answer a symmetric target without finding two messy roots separately.

Useful identities:

α2+β2=S2−2P,α3+β3=S3−3PS,\alpha^2+\beta^2=S^2-2P,\qquad \alpha^3+\beta^3=S^3-3PS,α2+β2=S2−2P,α3+β3=S3−3PS, (α−β)2=S2−4P=Δa2.\boxed{(\alpha-\beta)^2=S^2-4P=\frac{\Delta}{a^2}}.(α−β)2=S2−4P=a2Δ​​.

If P≠0P\ne0P=0, neither root is zero:

1α+1β=SP,1α2+1β2=S2−2PP2.\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac SP,\qquad \boxed{\frac1{\alpha^2}+\frac1{\beta^2}=\frac{S^2-2P}{P^2}}.α1​+β1​=PS​,α21​+β21​=P2S2−2P​​.

(α+β)2≤2(α2+β2).(\alpha+\beta)^2\le2(\alpha^2+\beta^2).(α+β)2≤2(α2+β2).

Concept C06 — A root equation becomes a rule for higher powers

Important for JEE Main. For a monic equation t2−St+P=0t^2-St+P=0t2−St+P=0, every root obeys

t2=St−P.t^2=St-P.t2=St−P.

Multiply by tn−2t^{n-2}tn−2 and add the equations for both roots. For Un=αn+βnU_n=\alpha^n+\beta^nUn​=αn+βn,

U0=2,U1=S,Un=SUn−1−PUn−2(n≥2).\boxed{U_0=2,\quad U_1=S,\quad U_n=SU_{n-1}-PU_{n-2}\quad(n\ge2)}.U0​=2,U1​=S,Un​=SUn−1​−PUn−2​(n≥2)​.

The same recurrence holds for differences an=αn−βna_n=\alpha^n-\beta^nan​=αn−βn. It follows by subtraction instead of addition, with a0=0a_0=0a0​=0 and a1=α−βa_1=\alpha-\betaa1​=α−β.

Why this helps: it replaces high powers by two previous values. For t2−t−1=0t^2-t-1=0t2−t−1=0, the rule is simply Un=Un−1+Un−2U_n=U_{n-1}+U_{n-2}Un​=Un−1​+Un−2​.

U2n=Un2−2Pn.\boxed{U_{2n}=U_n^2-2P^n}.U2n​=Un2​−2Pn​.

Before dividing by a power sum or difference, prove its denominator is nonzero.

Concept C07 — A quadratic inequality asks where the graph is above or below zero

Important for JEE Main. Suppose the real roots are r1<r2r_1<r_2r1​<r2​. Then

f(x)=a(x−r1)(x−r2).f(x)=a(x-r_1)(x-r_2).f(x)=a(x−r1​)(x−r2​).

Outside the two roots, the factors have the same sign. Between them, the factors have opposite signs.

For a>0a>0a>0:

f(x)≤0  ⟺  r1≤x≤r2,f(x)≥0  ⟺  x≤r1 or x≥r2.\boxed{f(x)\le0\iff r_1\le x\le r_2},\qquad \boxed{f(x)\ge0\iff x\le r_1\text{ or }x\ge r_2}.f(x)≤0⟺r1​≤x≤r2​​,f(x)≥0⟺x≤r1​ or x≥r2​​.

Use open endpoints for strict inequalities. If a<0a<0a<0, reverse the sign regions.

Special cases matter.

  • If Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0, the expression has the sign of aaa everywhere.
  • If Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0, it is a(x−h)2a(x-h)^2a(x−h)2: it touches zero but does not change sign there.
  • A strict inequality excludes roots; a non-strict one may include them.

For integers in a closed integer-ended interval [L,U][L,U][L,U], count U−L+1U-L+1U−L+1. The +1+1+1 includes both endpoints. For noninteger boundaries, first identify the first and last allowed integers, respecting open endpoints.

Concept C08 — Rational inequalities: signs and forbidden points

Important for JEE Main. A denominator cannot be zero, even in a non-strict inequality.

For

(x−1)(x−2)x−3≥0,\frac{(x-1)(x-2)}{x-3}\ge0,x−3(x−1)(x−2)​≥0,

mark the numerator zeros 1,21,21,2 and forbidden point 333. Between neighbouring marked values, each factor keeps a fixed sign.

Read the chart: multiply or divide the factor signs. Include 1,21,21,2 because they give a defined zero. Exclude 333 because no value exists there.

Why not multiply directly by x−3x-3x−3? It may be positive or negative. Multiplying an inequality by a negative quantity reverses its direction. You would need separate cases.

An alternative is to multiply by the definitely positive square (x−3)2(x-3)^2(x−3)2 on the domain x≠3x\ne3x=3:

(x−1)(x−2)x−3≥0  ⟺  (x−1)(x−2)(x−3)≥0,x≠3.\frac{(x-1)(x-2)}{x-3}\ge0 \iff (x-1)(x-2)(x-3)\ge0,\quad x\ne3.x−3(x−1)(x−2)​≥0⟺(x−1)(x−2)(x−3)≥0,x=3.

Odd and even multiplicity. A simple factor changes sign when crossing its zero. A squared factor such as (x−1)2(x-1)^2(x−1)2 does not. Do not automatically alternate signs at every marked point without checking the powers.

Cancellation does not fill a hole. If you cancel an x−3x-3x−3 factor from a rational expression, the original exclusion x≠3x\ne3x=3 still belongs to the answer. List the original domain before simplifying.

y2−(u+v)y+uv=0.\boxed{y^2-(u+v)y+uv=0}.y2−(u+v)y+uv=0​.

Concept C10 — A common root belongs to both equations

Important for JEE Main. If rrr is a common root, then both f(r)=0f(r)=0f(r)=0 and g(r)=0g(r)=0g(r)=0. Any suitable sum or difference of these two equations must also be zero.

If the leading coefficients match, subtracting often removes r2r^2r2. Example:

r2+pr+q=0,r2+qr+p=0.r^2+pr+q=0,\qquad r^2+qr+p=0.r2+pr+q=0,r2+qr+p=0.

Subtract:

(p−q)r+(q−p)=0⟹(p−q)(r−1)=0.(p-q)r+(q-p)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad(p-q)(r-1)=0.(p−q)r+(q−p)=0⟹(p−q)(r−1)=0.

If p≠qp\ne qp=q, then r=1r=1r=1. Substitute it into either original equation to obtain the coefficient condition.

If the leading coefficients differ, first multiply the equations by constants so their squared terms cancel. If the resulting linear coefficient also vanishes, inspect what remains: the equations may be proportional, or they may be inconsistent. Do not divide by an expression that could be zero.

Why not solve both quadratics first? That works, but can create four radical expressions and an unnecessary matching problem. Elimination uses the fact that the same input solves both.

Concept C11 — Extreme values: finish the square and check the allowed input

Important for JEE Main. Write

f(x)=a(x−h)2+v.f(x)=a(x-h)^2+v.f(x)=a(x−h)2+v.

On all real inputs, if a>0a>0a>0, its minimum is vvv at x=hx=hx=h and its range is [v,∞)[v,\infty)[v,∞). It has no finite maximum. If a<0a<0a<0, its maximum is vvv at hhh and its range is (−∞,v](-\infty,v](−∞,v]; it has no finite minimum.

A restricted domain changes this. On a closed interval, check the endpoints and the vertex if it belongs to the interval. For an upward parabola the maximum is at an endpoint; the minimum is at the vertex if allowed, otherwise at the nearer endpoint.

A hidden quadratic needs its new domain.

Substitution Allowed new values
t=x2t=x^2t=x2 or t=∣x∣t=|x|t=∣x∣ t≥0t\ge0t≥0
t=2xt=2^xt=2x t>0t>0t>0
t=x+1/xt=x+1/xt=x+1/x, real x≠0x\ne0x=0 t≤−2t\le-2t≤−2 or t≥2t\ge2t≥2

Every value in the last row occurs: x2−tx+1=0x^2-tx+1=0x2−tx+1=0 has real, nonzero roots exactly when t2≥4t^2\ge4t2≥4.

For the last row, (x−1)2≥0(x-1)^2\ge0(x−1)2≥0 gives the positive-xxx bound; applying it to −x-x−x gives the negative-xxx bound. Do not include the gap (−2,2)(-2,2)(−2,2).

Example:

4x−2x+3+20=(2x)2−8(2x)+20.4^x-2^{x+3}+20=(2^x)^2-8(2^x)+20.4x−2x+3+20=(2x)2−8(2x)+20.

t2−8t+20=(t−4)2+4.t^2-8t+20=(t-4)^2+4.t2−8t+20=(t−4)2+4.

The minimum 444 is attained because t=4t=4t=4 is allowed, with original input x=2x=2x=2.

What if the best new value is forbidden? For (2x+1)2+4(2^x+1)^2+4(2x+1)2+4, the new domain is still t>0t>0t>0. The expression is greater than 555 and approaches 555 as t→0+t\to0^+t→0+. It has infimum 555 but no attained minimum. “Infimum” means the greatest lower bound; a minimum must also be reached.

Cauchy–Schwarz connection — Important for JEE Main. For real x,yx,yx,y, x2+y2≥(x+y)2/2x^2+y^2\ge(x+y)^2/2x2+y2≥(x+y)2/2. If a question fixes a sum, a square inequality may find an extreme more directly than solving for both numbers.

Concept C12 — Modulus: choose a nonnegative variable or a distance picture

Important for JEE Main. For a real number,

∣x∣={x,x≥0,−x,x<0.|x|=\begin{cases}x,&x\ge0,\\-x,&x<0.\end{cases}∣x∣={x,−x,​x≥0,x<0.​

If the expression contains x2x^2x2 and ∣x∣|x|∣x∣, notice that x2=∣x∣2x^2=|x|^2x2=∣x∣2. Put t=∣x∣≥0t=|x|\ge0t=∣x∣≥0.

For example,

x2−4∣x∣+3=0  ⟺  t2−4t+3=0,t≥0.x^2-4|x|+3=0 \iff t^2-4t+3=0,\quad t\ge0.x2−4∣x∣+3=0⟺t2−4t+3=0,t≥0.

If t=1t=1t=1 or 333, restore x=±1,±3x=\pm1,\pm3x=±1,±3. A positive ttt gives two xxx values; t=0t=0t=0 gives only one; a negative candidate ttt gives none.

Distance view: ∣x−a∣|x-a|∣x−a∣ is the distance of the number xxx from aaa on a real number line.

For a<ba<ba<b,

∣x−a∣+∣x−b∣={a+b−2x,x≤a,b−a,a≤x≤b,2x−a−b,x≥b.|x-a|+|x-b| =\begin{cases} a+b-2x,&x\le a,\\ b-a,&a\le x\le b,\\ 2x-a-b,&x\ge b. \end{cases}∣x−a∣+∣x−b∣=⎩⎨⎧​a+b−2x,b−a,2x−a−b,​x≤a,a≤x≤b,x≥b.​

Between the two fixed points, one distance increases exactly as the other decreases. The total stays b−ab-ab−a. Outside, moving further adds to both distances.

A compact equivalent identity is

∣x−a∣+∣x−b∣=2max⁡(∣x−a+b2∣,b−a2).\boxed{|x-a|+|x-b| =2\max\left(\left|x-\frac{a+b}{2}\right|,\frac{b-a}{2}\right)}.∣x−a∣+∣x−b∣=2max(​x−2a+b​​,2b−a​)​.

Use the three pieces or the picture before trying to memorize this compact version.

Do not square a modulus equation without checking the effect. ∣g(x)∣=h(x)|g(x)|=h(x)∣g(x)∣=h(x) first needs h(x)≥0h(x)\ge0h(x)≥0. It then gives g(x)=h(x)g(x)=h(x)g(x)=h(x) or g(x)=−h(x)g(x)=-h(x)g(x)=−h(x). Keep the sign cases and domain.

Concept C13 — Square-root equations: squaring is a candidate-producing step

Important for JEE Main. A principal real square root is nonnegative. Thus

g(x)=h(x)\sqrt{g(x)}=h(x)g(x)​=h(x)

requires both

g(x)≥0,h(x)≥0.g(x)\ge0,\qquad h(x)\ge0.g(x)≥0,h(x)≥0.

Only after that should we square:

g(x)=h(x)2.g(x)=h(x)^2.g(x)=h(x)2.

Squaring forgets the sign of the right side. A candidate with h(x)<0h(x)<0h(x)<0 can solve the squared equation and still fail the original one.

For x+5=x−1\sqrt{x+5}=x-1x+5​=x−1, first get x≥1x\ge1x≥1. Squaring gives x=4,−1x=4,-1x=4,−1; only 444 survives. This is why the sum of roots of the squared polynomial is not automatically the requested sum of original solutions.

Graph view: a solution is an intersection of the two original graphs. The graph helps identify the correct sign and number of solutions; substitution gives the exact check.

Concept C14 — Real, rational, irrational, and conjugate roots

Important for JEE Main. The discriminant determines realness. Rationality needs an additional coefficient condition.

For rational coefficients, real roots are rational exactly when Δ\sqrt\DeltaΔ​ is rational. With integer coefficients, this means Δ\DeltaΔ is a nonnegative perfect-square integer. An integer root also needs

−b±Δ2a\frac{-b\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2a}2a−b±Δ​​

to be an integer; check the division, not only the square root.

For integer coefficients and a rational root p/qp/qp/q in lowest terms, ppp divides ccc and qqq divides aaa. This is the rational-root test. If c=0c=0c=0, check the root 000 first and factor out xxx.

Complex conjugates need real coefficients. If u+ivu+ivu+iv is a nonreal root, conjugating the whole equation with real coefficients proves that u−ivu-ivu−iv is a root too.

Surd conjugates need rational coefficients. If p+qdp+q\sqrt dp+qd​ is a root of a quadratic with rational coefficients, where p,qp,qp,q are rational, q≠0q\ne0q=0, and ddd is a positive nonsquare integer, then p−qdp-q\sqrt dp−qd​ is also a root.

Why? Substitution gives a rational part plus a rational multiple of d\sqrt dd​. The two parts must vanish separately; otherwise d\sqrt dd​ would be rational. Reversing the sign of d\sqrt dd​ still gives zero.

For source Q12's root 2+32+\sqrt32+3​,

a(2+3)2+b(2+3)+c=(7a+2b+c)+(4a+b)3.a(2+\sqrt3)^2+b(2+\sqrt3)+c =(7a+2b+c)+(4a+b)\sqrt3.a(2+3​)2+b(2+3​)+c=(7a+2b+c)+(4a+b)3​.

Both rational coefficients must be zero. Replacing +3+\sqrt3+3​ by −3-\sqrt3−3​ then also gives zero.

Do not weaken “rational” to “real.” The real-coefficient equation x2−(2+3)x=0x^2-(2+\sqrt3)x=0x2−(2+3​)x=0 has roots 0,2+30,2+\sqrt30,2+3​, not the surd pair. Rational and real are different requirements.

Concept C15 — Where are the roots? Use the simplest available view

Important for JEE Main. If the roots are already easy, compare them with the interval directly.

For

x2−2kx+k2−1=(x−k)2−1,x^2-2kx+k^2-1=(x-k)^2-1,x2−2kx+k2−1=(x−k)2−1,

the roots are k−1,k+1k-1,k+1k−1,k+1. Both are in (−2,4)(-2,4)(−2,4) exactly when

−2<k−1,k+1<4⟹−1<k<3.-2<k-1,\qquad k+1<4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -1<k<3.−2<k−1,k+1<4⟹−1<k<3.

When explicit roots are messy, use the graph. Let h=−b/(2a)h=-b/(2a)h=−b/(2a) and use f(x)/af(x)/af(x)/a, which always opens upward.

For example, (x−2)2−1(x-2)^2-1(x−2)2−1 has roots 1,31,31,3 inside (0,4)(0,4)(0,4). Its vertex input 222 is between the boundaries, and both boundary outputs are 3>03>03>0.

For both real roots strictly inside (L,U)(L,U)(L,U):

Δ≥0,L<h<U,f(L)a>0,f(U)a>0.\boxed{\Delta\ge0,\quad L<h<U,\quad \frac{f(L)}a>0,\quad\frac{f(U)}a>0}.Δ≥0,L<h<U,af(L)​>0,af(U)​>0​.

The vertex lies between the boundaries, while both boundary heights lie above the axis. If roots must be distinct, use Δ>0\Delta>0Δ>0. For both roots in the closed interval [L,U][L,U][L,U], replace the endpoint/vertex strict inequalities by non-strict ones.

For both roots to the right of ttt:

Δ≥0,h>t,f(t)/a>0.\Delta\ge0,\quad h>t,\quad f(t)/a>0.Δ≥0,h>t,f(t)/a>0.

For both to the left, use h<th<th<t. If one root is strictly on each side of ttt, then f(t)/a<0f(t)/a<0f(t)/a<0; this already gives two distinct real roots.

Opposite nonzero signs of f(L)f(L)f(L) and f(U)f(U)f(U) guarantee exactly one crossing in (L,U)(L,U)(L,U) for a quadratic. Endpoint roots and a repeated touching root need separate treatment; do not use the sign-change test as a universal description of every “one root” wording.

Parameter checklist: real roots → requested sign/location → strict or included boundaries → degree loss. Intersect the conditions; do not choose just the easiest one.

Concept C16 — Rational ranges: numerator and denominator share the same input

Important for JEE Main. In

f(x)=x2−3x+4x2+3x+4,f(x)=\frac{x^2-3x+4}{x^2+3x+4},f(x)=x2+3x+4x2−3x+4​,

the shared part is x2+4x^2+4x2+4, and the 3x3x3x sign changes. This resembles the repeated-pattern range question in Chapter 1.

D=x2+3x+4=(x+3/2)2+7/4>0.D=x^2+3x+4=(x+3/2)^2+7/4>0.D=x2+3x+4=(x+3/2)2+7/4>0.

The squares (x−2)2≥0(x-2)^2\ge0(x−2)2≥0 and (x+2)2≥0(x+2)^2\ge0(x+2)2≥0 give

−34≤u≤34.-\frac34\le u\le\frac34.−43​≤u≤43​.

Thus 1+u∈[1/4,7/4]1+u\in[1/4,7/4]1+u∈[1/4,7/4], so

f=−1+21+u∈[1/7,7].f=-1+\frac2{1+u}\in[1/7,7].f=−1+1+u2​∈[1/7,7].

Another possible approach — solve backwards. Set y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) and rearrange to

(y−1)x2+3(y+1)x+4(y−1)=0.(y-1)x^2+3(y+1)x+4(y-1)=0.(y−1)x2+3(y+1)x+4(y−1)=0.

For y≠1y\ne1y=1, real inputs require discriminant

9(y+1)2−16(y−1)2=(7−y)(7y−1)≥0.9(y+1)^2-16(y-1)^2=(7-y)(7y-1)\ge0.9(y+1)2−16(y−1)2=(7−y)(7y−1)≥0.

The case y=1y=1y=1 becomes linear and must be checked separately. A discriminant in the output variable gives possible outputs; original denominator restrictions must still be tested. Here the denominator is always positive.

Why not maximize numerator and minimize denominator separately? Their best inputs may differ. The same xxx controls both. Preserve their connection.

Concept C17 — When does a real power equal one?

Useful for the supplied Q20; domain checks are Important for JEE Main. A variable-base power should not be treated as a polynomial.

For a positive base A>0A>0A>0,

AB=1  ⟺  A=1 or B=0.\boxed{A^B=1\iff A=1\text{ or }B=0}.AB=1⟺A=1 or B=0​.

In the exponent-zero case the base must be nonzero; 000^000 is not accepted. A zero base never produces 111 under ordinary real-power rules.

A negative base is not defined for every real exponent. Integer exponents are allowed; some rational exponents in lowest terms are allowed when the denominator is odd. A nonzero exponent can produce 111 at a negative base only when that base is −1-1−1, with an allowed exponent giving a positive sign.

For an integer exponent,

(−1)B=1  ⟺  B is even.\boxed{(-1)^B=1\iff B\text{ is even}}.(−1)B=1⟺B is even​.

For an allowed rational exponent B=p/qB=p/qB=p/q in lowest terms with odd qqq, the numerator ppp must be even. Do not present “even integer” as the only possible case for every real-power problem.

In Q20, solving the base-−1-1−1 condition gives only x=2,3x=2,3x=2,3, whose exponents are integers −48,−39-48,-39−48,−39. Thus the ordinary even-integer check fully resolves that branch. Each candidate must be tested in its own base/exponent case. Combine the cases as a set; if one input appears twice, count it only once.

The source includes valid negative-base integer powers. If a question explicitly restricts the base to be positive, follow that narrower domain instead.

These are method cues, not measured frequency ranks.

High powers of roots Turn the root equation into a recurrence.
Coefficient sum zero Try input 111; alternating sum zero suggests −1-1−1.
Common root Eliminate the squared term at that same root.

“Both roots negative” Realness, negative sum, positive product.
“Positive for every real input” Opening direction and no real zeros; handle degree loss.

x2x^2x2 and ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ Use t=∣x∣≥0t=|x|\ge0t=∣x∣≥0; restore signs.
A root equation Nonnegative right side before squaring; check original equation.
Numerator/denominator share a pattern One bounded quantity or a backward discriminant.
Variable base raised to a variable power Separate base/exponent cases and retain real-power domain.

Question 1 — The target is a symmetric sum

PDF page 14 | MCQ | Notes: C05–C06

If α,β\alpha,\betaα,β are the roots of x2−5x+3=0x^2-5x+3=0x2−5x+3=0, then α3+β3\alpha^3+\beta^3α3+β3 equals

  • (b) 110110110
  • (c) 808080
  • (d) 656565

Notice the target: both cubes are added. The cube-of-a-sum identity contains exactly that group:

(α+β)3=α3+β3+3αβ(α+β).(\alpha+\beta)^3 =\alpha^3+\beta^3+3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta).(α+β)3=α3+β3+3αβ(α+β).

From the equation, S=5S=5S=5 and P=3P=3P=3. Rearrange only the part needed:

α3+β3=S3−3PS=125−45=80(c).\alpha^3+\beta^3=S^3-3PS =125-45=\boxed{80}\qquad\text{(c)}.α3+β3=S3−3PS=125−45=80​(c).

Why this route? Finding the two irrational roots separately works, but their cube expansions would later cancel. Sum/product uses the cancellation before calculating.

Check by a second identity: U2=S2−2P=19U_2=S^2-2P=19U2​=S2−2P=19, so the root recurrence gives U3=SU2−PU1=5(19)−3(5)=80U_3=SU_2-PU_1=5(19)-3(5)=80U3​=SU2​−PU1​=5(19)−3(5)=80.

(m−6)(m+6)>0.(m-6)(m+6)>0.(m−6)(m+6)>0.

m<−6 or m>6(a).\boxed{m<-6\text{ or }m>6}\qquad\text{(a)}.m<−6 or m>6​(a).

4.\boxed{4}.4​.

Question 4 — A common root survives subtraction

PDF page 14 | MCQ | Notes: C10

If x2+px+q=0x^2+px+q=0x2+px+q=0 and x2+qx+p=0x^2+qx+p=0x2+qx+p=0 (p≠q)(p\ne q)(p=q) have a common root, then p+qp+qp+q equals

  • (a) 111
  • (b) 000
  • (c) 222
  • (d) −1-1−1

Call the common root rrr. The same rrr solves both equations:

r2+pr+q=0,r2+qr+p=0.r^2+pr+q=0,\qquad r^2+qr+p=0.r2+pr+q=0,r2+qr+p=0.

Subtract to remove the squared term:

(p−q)(r−1)=0.(p-q)(r-1)=0.(p−q)(r−1)=0.

The given p≠qp\ne qp=q allows division by p−qp-qp−q, so r=1r=1r=1. Substitute into an original equation:

1+p+q=0⟹p+q=−1(d).1+p+q=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{p+q=-1}\qquad\text{(d)}.1+p+q=0⟹p+q=−1​(d).

Check: if p+q=−1p+q=-1p+q=−1, input 111 makes both polynomials zero. The condition is consistent.

Solving each quadratic separately would introduce radicals and a root-matching step. Subtraction is better here because the leading terms already match.

Question 5 — Build a new equation from a new sum and product

PDF page 14 | MCQ | Notes: C09

The equation whose roots are the squares of the roots of x2−3x+1=0x^2-3x+1=0x2−3x+1=0 is

  • (a) 111
  • (b) 222
  • (c) 444
  • (d) 555

The unusual clue is that the root names are also coefficient names. Apply both Viète relations to exactly those two roots:

a+b=−a,ab=b.a+b=-a,\qquad ab=b.a+b=−a,ab=b.

Since b≠0b\ne0b=0, divide the product equation by bbb: a=1a=1a=1. The sum relation gives b=−2a=−2b=-2a=-2b=−2a=−2.

Therefore

a2+b2=1+4=5(d).\boxed{a^2+b^2=1+4=5}\qquad\text{(d)}.a2+b2=1+4=5​(d).

Check the complete root pair: x2+x−2=(x−1)(x+2)x^2+x-2=(x-1)(x+2)x2+x−2=(x−1)(x+2) has exactly the claimed roots a=1,b=−2a=1,b=-2a=1,b=−2. The nonzero condition is what justified division by bbb.

Question 20 — An expression to a power equals one: separate the cases

PDF page 16 | Numerical value | Notes: C17

The sum of all real values of xxx satisfying (x2−5x+5)x2+4x−60=1(x^2-5x+5)^{x^2+4x-60}=1(x2−5x+5)x2+4x−60=1 is ____.

A power equals one through special base/exponent cases. Call the base A=x2−5x+5A=x^2-5x+5A=x2−5x+5 and exponent B=x2+4x−60B=x^2+4x-60B=x2+4x−60.

For a positive base, A=1A=1A=1 or B=0B=0B=0 is needed. A negative base can also work here when A=−1A=-1A=−1 and its candidate exponent is an even integer. A zero base never gives 111.

Case 1: base 111.

x2−5x+5=1  ⟺  (x−1)(x−4)=0.x^2-5x+5=1 \iff(x-1)(x-4)=0.x2−5x+5=1⟺(x−1)(x−4)=0.

This gives x=1,4x=1,4x=1,4, both valid: 111 to any real exponent is 111.

Case 2: exponent 000, with nonzero base.

x2+4x−60=(x+10)(x−6)=0.x^2+4x-60=(x+10)(x-6)=0.x2+4x−60=(x+10)(x−6)=0.

This gives x=−10,6x=-10,6x=−10,6. Their bases are respectively 155,11155,11155,11, both nonzero, so both work.

Case 3: base −1-1−1.

x2−5x+5=−1  ⟺  (x−2)(x−3)=0.x^2-5x+5=-1 \iff(x-2)(x-3)=0.x2−5x+5=−1⟺(x−2)(x−3)=0.

At x=2x=2x=2, B=−48B=-48B=−48, and (−1)−48=1(-1)^{-48}=1(−1)−48=1, so it works. At x=3x=3x=3, B=−39B=-39B=−39, and (−1)−39=−1(-1)^{-39}=-1(−1)−39=−1, so it fails.

The complete solution set is {−10,1,2,4,6}\{-10,1,2,4,6\}{−10,1,2,4,6}, whose sum is

−10+1+2+4+6=3.\boxed{-10+1+2+4+6=3}.−10+1+2+4+6=3​.

Domain check: we used ordinary real/integer powers at these candidates. No unsupported negative-base irrational power was used. For a nonzero real exponent at any allowed negative base other than −1-1−1, the magnitude cannot be 111; the only extra negative-base candidates were already in Case 3. Count the union of cases, not duplicates.

Question 22 — A ratio suggests writing both roots with one scale

PDF page 16 | MCQ | Notes: C05

If the roots of x2−10x+k=0x^2-10x+k=0x2−10x+k=0 are in the ratio 2:32:32:3, then kkk equals

Question 23 — No real roots does not decide whether the graph is above or below

PDF page 16 | MCQ | Notes: C03, C04

The expression (m+1)x2−2(m−1)x+3(m−1)(m+1)x^2-2(m-1)x+3(m-1)(m+1)x2−2(m−1)x+3(m−1) is positive for all real xxx if

  • (a) m<−2m<-2m<−2
  • (b) m>−1m>-1m>−1
  • (c) m<−2m<-2m<−2 or m>1m>1m>1
  • (d) m>1m>1m>1

“Positive for all real xxx” needs the whole graph above the axis. A genuine quadratic must open upward and have no real zeros:

m+1>0,Δ<0.m+1>0,\qquad\Delta<0.m+1>0,Δ<0.

Compute the discriminant carefully, including the −2-2−2 in the linear coefficient:

Δ=[−2(m−1)]2−4(m+1) 3(m−1)=−8(m−1)(m+2).\begin{aligned} \Delta &=[-2(m-1)]^2-4(m+1)\,3(m-1)\\ &=-8(m-1)(m+2). \end{aligned}Δ​=[−2(m−1)]2−4(m+1)3(m−1)=−8(m−1)(m+2).​

Thus Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0 gives m<−2m<-2m<−2 or m>1m>1m>1. Intersect with m>−1m>-1m>−1:

m>1(d).\boxed{m>1}\qquad\text{(d)}.m>1​(d).

Check degree loss and strictness: at m=−1m=-1m=−1, the expression is 4x−64x-64x−6, not positive everywhere. At m=1m=1m=1, it is 2x22x^22x2, which equals zero at x=0x=0x=0, so it fails strict positivity.

Why option (c) fails: when m<−2m<-2m<−2, the graph opens downward and stays negative. A negative discriminant cannot decide the sign without the leading coefficient.

Question 24 — Two moduli are two distances on a number line

PDF page 16 | MCQ | Notes: C12

The number of integers xxx satisfying ∣x−1∣+∣x−3∣≤4|x-1|+|x-3|\le4∣x−1∣+∣x−3∣≤4 is

  • (b) 333
  • (c) 555
  • (d) 666

Read each modulus as a distance. We want the sum of distances from 111 and 333 to be at most 444.

Between 111 and 333, the distance sum is the fixed gap 222, so that entire segment is allowed.

To the left, x≤1x\le1x≤1:

∣x−1∣+∣x−3∣=4−2x≤4⟹x≥0.|x-1|+|x-3|=4-2x\le4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\ge0.∣x−1∣+∣x−3∣=4−2x≤4⟹x≥0.

To the right, x≥3x\ge3x≥3:

∣x−1∣+∣x−3∣=2x−4≤4⟹x≤4.|x-1|+|x-3|=2x-4\le4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\le4.∣x−1∣+∣x−3∣=2x−4≤4⟹x≤4.

The combined allowed interval is [0,4][0,4][0,4]. Its integers are 0,1,2,3,40,1,2,3,40,1,2,3,4:

5(c).\boxed{5}\qquad\text{(c)}.5​(c).

Another possible approach — centre the picture at 222. Set u=x−2u=x-2u=x−2. Then ∣u+1∣+∣u−1∣=2max⁡(∣u∣,1)≤4|u+1|+|u-1|=2\max(|u|,1)\le4∣u+1∣+∣u−1∣=2max(∣u∣,1)≤4, equivalent to ∣u∣≤2|u|\le2∣u∣≤2. Hence 0≤x≤40\le x\le40≤x≤4. Use this compact identity after understanding the flat middle and rising outer pieces.

Coverage and source notes

All 252525 source questions are included in order, with their original 181818 MCQ and 777 numerical-value formats. Root formation, signs, domain checks, equality cases, parameter degeneracies, and useful prerequisites are taught before the questions.

Q20 is interpreted using ordinary real powers wherever they are defined, including the valid negative-base integer-power candidate. This convention is explicit before the solution. All independently checked results agree with the source key.

The recent-weightage audit is a recount of 494949 distinct archive-category cards for 202420242024–202620262026, not an independent full-paper reclassification. It is not an exhaustive 202020202020–202620262026 formula-frequency audit, and the method-cue table is not a measured model ranking.
